introduction-how-reliable-is-reliable-en.core: 100% reliability is impossible and not worth pursuing: each extra nine costs roughly ten times more, and users can't tell 99.99% from 100% because their own networks fail more often. SRE picks a target that keeps users happy, measures against it, and treats the gap below 100% as a budget to spend on shipping features and taking risks.

first_principles.problem: A team chases zero incidents, freezes releases, and still can't explain to leadership whether the service is 'reliable enough'.
derivation: Use the budget to **balance speed and stability**.

analogy.title: A household budget for risk
analogy.story: You don't refuse to spend money; you decide how much you can afford and track it.
analogy.breaks: Money can be borrowed; error budgets can't be paid back early.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Makes the cost of each nine concrete.

check.q: Why is 100% the wrong reliability target?
check.a: It's unachievable and exponentially costly, and users can't perceive the difference beyond a point, so it blocks all change for no benefit.

sli-service-level-indicator-the-measurem.core: An SLI is a ratio of good events to valid events, measured as close to the user as possible: the share of requests that succeeded, the share faster than 300 ms, the share of records fresh within 10 minutes. Good SLIs map to user happiness, are precisely defined (what counts as good, which requests are excluded), and come from load balancer logs, server metrics, client telemetry or synthetic probes.

first_principles.problem: A dashboard shows CPU and memory but nobody can say what fraction of user checkouts actually succeeded.
truths: Measurement point changes what you see.

analogy.title: A restaurant's 'meals served on time and correct' ratio
analogy.story: Kitchen temperature doesn't matter to diners; the share of meals right and on time does.
analogy.breaks: Diners complain; most users silently leave.

code.text:
# availability: non-5xx share
sum(rate(http_requests_total{service="checkout",code!~"5.."}[30d]))
/ sum(rate(http_requests_total{service="checkout"}[30d]))
# latency: share under 300 ms
sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{service="checkout",le="0.3"}[30d]))
/ sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_count{service="checkout"}[30d]))

check.q: Why express SLIs as ratios rather than raw error counts?
check.a: Ratios normalise for traffic volume, so the indicator is comparable across busy and quiet periods.

slo-service-level-objective-the-goal.core: An SLO is a target value for an SLI over a time window: 99.9% of checkout requests succeed over a rolling 28 days, or 95% complete under 300 ms. Set it from user needs and historical performance, not aspiration. It must be achievable but meaningful, and reviewed regularly. SLOs are internal engineering goals, stricter than any external SLA.

first_principles.problem: A team sets 99.999% because it 'sounds good', then misses it every month and everyone ignores it.
truths: Targets must be achievable to matter.

analogy.title: A train punctuality target
analogy.story: '95% of trains within 5 minutes' is realistic and measurable; 'every train exactly on time' is ignored.
analogy.breaks: Train targets are public; SLOs are internal and can be tuned.

code.text:
apiVersion: openslo/v1
kind: SLO
metadata: { name: checkout-availability }
spec:
  service: checkout
  timeWindow: [{ duration: 28d, isRolling: true }]
  budgetingMethod: Occurrences
  objectives: [{ displayName: success, target: 0.999 }]
  indicatorRef: checkout-non-5xx-ratio

check.q: Why should an SLO usually be stricter than the external SLA?
check.a: So you get early warning and room to react before breaching the contractual promise.

sla-service-level-agreement-the-contract.core: An SLA is a business contract with customers: if availability falls below X% in a billing period, the provider owes service credits or refunds. It is written by legal and business teams, is usually looser than the internal SLO, defines measurement and exclusions precisely, and has financial consequences. Engineering manages to the SLO so the SLA is never breached.

first_principles.problem: Sales promises 99.99% in a contract while the service's internal SLO is 99.9%.

analogy.title: A warranty vs the factory's quality target
analogy.story: The factory aims for 99.9% defect-free; the warranty only promises replacement if something fails in a year.
analogy.breaks: Warranties are per product; SLAs aggregate across a billing period.

check.q: Can your SLA be stronger than your cloud provider's SLA for a dependency you can't avoid?
check.a: Only with redundancy across providers or regions; otherwise you're promising more than your dependency guarantees.

the-error-budget-the-currency-of-risk.core: The error budget is 1 − SLO. A 99.9% SLO over 28 days allows 0.1% of requests to fail, about 40 minutes of full downtime. While budget remains, teams ship fast and experiment; when it's exhausted, policy shifts effort to reliability (release freeze, postmortem actions) until it recovers. It turns reliability-versus-velocity arguments into an objective, pre-agreed decision rule.

first_principles.problem: Product and SRE argue every week about whether a risky release should ship.
truths: Some failure is acceptable by design.

analogy.title: A monthly mobile data allowance
analogy.story: Stream freely while you have data left; once it's gone, you're careful until it resets.
analogy.breaks: Data allowances reset on a date; rolling budgets recover gradually.

example.title: Budget math
flow: Policy: ship only fixes until < 50% burned

check.q: What should happen when a service exhausts its error budget?
check.a: Per the agreed policy, prioritise reliability work and slow or freeze risky changes until the budget recovers.

burn-rates-and-multi-window-alerting.core: Burn rate is how fast you're consuming budget relative to plan: a burn rate of 1 uses exactly the whole budget over the window, and 14.4 would exhaust a 30-day budget in about 2 days. Multi-window, multi-burn-rate alerts page on a fast burn (14.4× over 1 h confirmed by 5 m) and ticket on a slow burn (6× over 6 h, or 1× over 3 days), catching both outages and slow degradation with few false alarms.

first_principles.problem: A static 'error rate > 1%' alert either pages for short blips or misses slow budget erosion.
truths: Short windows are noisy, long ones slow.

analogy.title: A fuel gauge with a range estimate
analogy.story: 'At this rate you'll run out in 50 miles' is more useful than 'fuel is below half'.
analogy.breaks: Fuel use is steady; error bursts are spiky, hence two windows.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Pages within minutes of a real outage, resets quickly after recovery.

code.text:
- alert: CheckoutErrorBudgetFastBurn
  expr: |
    (job:slo_errors:ratio_rate1h{service="checkout"} > 14.4 * 0.001)
    and
    (job:slo_errors:ratio_rate5m{service="checkout"} > 14.4 * 0.001)
  labels: { severity: page }
  annotations: { summary: "Checkout burning 2% of monthly budget per hour" }

check.q: Why combine a long and a short window in a burn-rate alert?
check.a: The long window ensures significant budget was consumed; the short window confirms it's still happening, so the alert stops quickly after recovery.
